abstract: Modern soybean (Glycine max) canopies carry more leaves than they need, so yield gains depend on using light more efficiently. Lines carrying the narrow-leaflet allele of GmJAG1 yield as much as broad leaflet lines despite having less leaf area. We asked whether leaflet shape raises canopy light capture or light-use efficiency. To separate the two, we simulated 530 measured plots of broad- and narrow-leaflet near isogenic lines at two sites in the Helios three-dimensional ray-tracing model. We compared these simulations with a one-dimensional model of identical leaf physiology and with field data, then mapped the traits by genome-wide association. In the simulations, both leaflet types absorbed similar fractions of light, but narrow-leaflet canopies had 4-7% higher light-use efficiency. The one-dimensional model recovered little to none of this gain, tying it to canopy structure, where narrow leaflets partitioned light more evenly among leaves at each depth. In the field, narrow lines matched broad-line yield with 12% less leaf area, and yield per unit leaf area (+13.7%) mapped to GmJAG1, as did leaflet shape and simulated traits. With less leaf area, narrow-leaflets canopies are thus predicted to absorb as much light as broad-leaflet canopies and use it more efficiently. As a heritable single-gene trait, leaflet shape could complement leaf-biochemical routes to improved photosynthesis.
